rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن عامر
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read waṭāʾ with kasra on wāw and a long vowel.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وابن عامر وطاء بكسر الواو والمد

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers pronounce waṭʾ with fatḥa on wāw, a still ṭāʾ, and no long vowel.
rows.anchor: والباقون وطأ بفتح الواو وسكون الطاء مقصورا

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة غير حفص وابن عامر ويعقوب
rows.claim: Kufans other than Ḥafṣ, plus Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb, read rabb al-mashriq in the genitive.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الكوفة غير حفص وابن عامر ويعقوب رب المشرق بالجر

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers pronounce rabb al-mashriq in the nominative.
rows.anchor: والباقون بالرفع وفي الشواذ قراءة عكرمة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: In a noncanonical reading, ʿIkrima lightens zāy and dāl and doubles mīm and thāʾ in al-Muzzammil and al-Muddaththir.
rows.anchor: قراءة عكرمة المزمل والمدثر خفيفة الزاي والدال مشددة الميم والثاء

rows.speaker: أبو السماك
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāk's noncanonical reading has ḍamma on the mīm of qum, possibly by assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقراءة أبي السماك قم الليل بضم الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With waṭāʾ, the phrase means greater concord: night prayer aligns hearing and heart because the mind is freer than in daytime; the reading is supported by 9:37.
rows.anchor: فمعناه مواطأة أي موافقة وملاءمة ومنه ليواطئوا عدة ما حرم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With waṭʾ, the phrase means night prayer is harder because night is normally a time of rest and quiet.
rows.anchor: ومن قال وطأ فالمعنى أنه أشق على الإنسان من القيام بالنهار

rows.speaker: أنس ومجاهد وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain aqwamu qīlan as more correct and sound speech because the mind is unoccupied.
rows.anchor: وأقوم قيلا أي أشد استقامة وصوابا لفراغ البال وانقطاع ما يشغله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line uses qawīm to mean upright or straight.
rows.anchor: ووقع بمستن القضاء قويم أي مستقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāshiʾat al-layl denotes the hours that arise successively through the night.
rows.anchor: والناشئة ما يحدث وينشأ من ساعات الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With nominative rabb, it may be a predicate of an omitted subject after the phrase is cut off.
rows.anchor: أنه لما قال واذكر اسم ربك قطعه من الأول فقال هو رب المشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, nominative rabb is a subject whose predicate is the sentence lā ilāha illā huwa.
rows.anchor: أن يكون مبتدأ وخبره الجملة التي هي لا إله إلا هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive reading follows the genitive in the preceding phrase ism rabbik.
rows.anchor: ومن جر فعلى اتباعه قوله { اسم ربك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the light-consonant reading, the object is omitted: the address means one who wraps or covers himself.
rows.anchor: فعلى حذف المفعول به يا أيها المزمل نفسه والمدثر نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muzzammil means a person wrapped in clothes; the tāʾ assimilates into the nearby, more audible zāy.
rows.anchor: المزمل المتزمل في ثيابه أدغم التاء في الزاي لأن الزاي قريبة المخرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word also applies to anything wrapped; al-Ṭabrisī cites Imruʾ al-Qays's line describing a wrapped figure.
rows.anchor: وكل شيء لفف فقد زمل قال امرؤ القيس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa and al-Shanfará's cited lines illustrate omission of a verb's object, as in the gloss that one guards and stores a conversation.
rows.anchor: أي تصون حديثا وتخزنه كقول الشنفرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A half is one of two equal portions, just as a third and quarter are portions of three and four; these fractions describe bodies and their parts.
rows.anchor: والنصف أحد قسمي الشيء المساوي للآخر في المقدار كما أن الثلث جزء من ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accidents and the eternal God are not divisible into halves or parts, since such descriptions concern composites.
rows.anchor: والعرض لا يوصف بالنصف والجزء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God one is praise because it signifies uniquely possessing attributes such as power, knowledge, and eternity in Himself.
rows.anchor: معنى قولنا إنه واحد اختصاصه بصفات لا يستحقها غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tartīl carefully articulates each letter as it deserves; rapid ḥadr is also good, but tartīl is encouraged here.
rows.anchor: والترتيل ترتيب الحروف على حقها في تلاوتها بتثبت فيها والحدر هو الإسراع فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilqāʾ is synonymous with talqiya, as when one poses a question to someone.
rows.anchor: والإلقاء مثل التلقية تقول ألقت على فلان مسألة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aqwamu means the most upright or sound in correctness.
rows.anchor: والأقوم الأخلص استقامة

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabḥ means movement or turning about, like a swimmer moving through water.
rows.anchor: والسبح التقلب ومنه السابح في الماء لتقلبه فيه

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: يحيى ابن يعمر والضحاك
rows.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read sabkhan with khāʾ, meaning expansion or spreading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ يحيى ابن يعمر والضحاك سبخا طويلا بالخاء ومعناه التوسعة

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb sabbakha means spreading cotton for carding; al-Akhṭal's cited line compares scattered dust to carded cotton.
rows.anchor: يقال: سبخت القطن إذا وسعته للندف

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet told ʿĀʾisha, who was praying against a thief, not to lighten or relieve her curse by supplication.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لعائشة

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab says sabḥ means restless movement and agitation, while sabkh means stillness.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب: السبح التردد والاضطراب والسبخ السكون

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying describes fever as heat from Hell and says to calm it with water.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabattul means severing oneself for God and devoting worship exclusively to Him; its root means cutting something off.
rows.anchor: والتبتل الانقطاع إلى الله عز وجل وإخلاص العبادة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-layl is an adverbial of time, and qaliilan is an accusative exception meaning a small part of the night is left without prayer.
rows.anchor: الليل نصب على الظرف إلا قليلا نصب على الاستثناء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses half of it as an apposition to al-layl, reinforcing it.
rows.anchor: إن نصفه بدل من الليل كما تقول ضربت زيدا رأسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command gives a range around half the night: reduce the half a little or increase it a little.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى قم نصف الليل أو انقص من نصف الليل أو زد على نصف الليل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes al-Muzzammil as the one wrapped in clothes.
rows.anchor: معناه يا أيها المتزمل بثيابه المتلفف بها عن قتادة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima explains the address as the one wrapped in the mantle of prophecy and bearing its burdens.
rows.anchor: بعباءة النبوة أي المتحمل لأثقالها عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says it means the sleeper, who had wrapped himself to sleep.
rows.anchor: معناه يا أيها النائم وكان قد تزمل للنوم عن السدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says he wrapped himself in fear when Gabriel first came, before he had preached anything; later he was addressed as prophet and messenger.
rows.anchor: كان يتزمل بالثياب في أول ما جاء به جبرائيل خوفا حتى أنس به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Standing through the night means praying at night.
rows.anchor: المعنى بالليل صل إلا قليلا من الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the main parsing, half of it apposes al-layl and specifies the exception.
rows.anchor: هو بدل من الليل فيكون بيانا للمستثنى منه أي قم نصف الليل

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes explain reducing as going down to one third and increasing as going up to two thirds.
rows.anchor: وقال المفسرون أو انقص من النصف قليلا إلى الثلث أو زد على النصف إلى الثلثين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parsing makes half of it an apposition to qaliil, specifying the exception with the same practical meaning.
rows.anchor: إن نصفه بدل من القليل فيكون بيانا للمستثنى والمعنى فيهما سواء

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: A report from al-Ṣādiq supports that parsing: the little is half, then slightly less or more than that amount.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن الصادق ع قال القليل النصف أو أنقص من القليل قليلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root means cutting off; an irrevocable endowment is separated from its donor, and Mary is called al-Batūl for devotion to God.
rows.anchor: وأصله من تبلت الشيء قطعته وصدقة بتة بتلة أي بائنة مقطوعة

rows.speaker: الإمام علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: One interpretation excepts a few nights of valid excuse, such as illness, overpowering sleep, or eye trouble.
rows.anchor: ذكره الإمام علي بن أبي طالب ع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God left the Prophet free to choose the night hours, and he and a group of believers prayed for these amounts.
rows.anchor: خير الله سبحانه نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم في هذه الساعات القيام بالليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The measure was difficult: some believers could not track how long they had prayed and stayed up all night for fear of falling short.
rows.anchor: فكان الرجل منهم لا يدري كم صلى وكم بقي من الليل فكان يقوم الليل كله

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says night prayer was obligatory at the surah's beginning; the Prophet and companions performed it for a year, then the closing passage eased it and made it voluntary.
rows.anchor: قلت لعائشة انبئيني عن قيام رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says ten years elapsed between the surah's opening and its passage of relief.
rows.anchor: كان بين أول السورة وآخرها الذي نزل فيه التخفيف عشر سنين عن سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān and Muqātil place the command in Mecca before the five prayers and say those prayers abrogated it.
rows.anchor: كان هذا بمكة قبل فرض الصلوات الخمس ثم نسخ بالخمس عن ابن كيسان ومقاتل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a year separated the surah's beginning and end, and the believers initially prayed about as long as in Ramadan.
rows.anchor: كانوا يقومون نحوا من قيامهم في شهر رمضان

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrima say the final verse abrogated the first.
rows.anchor: إن الآية الأخيرة نسخت الأولى عن الحسن وعكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses do not require abrogation; the better reading is that night prayer is strongly recommended, not obligatory.
rows.anchor: وليس في ظاهر الآيات ما يقتضي النسخ فالأولى أن يكون الكلام على ظاهره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says to articulate the Qurʾan clearly and read unhurriedly in sets of three, four, or five verses.
rows.anchor: ثلاث آيات وأربعا وخمسا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says clarity requires not rushing: every letter must be fully articulated and given its due.
rows.anchor: والبيان لا يتم بأن تعجل في القرآن إنما يتم بأن تبين جميع الحروف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās told Abū Ḥamza he preferred a measured reading of al-Baqara to reciting the whole Qurʾan.
rows.anchor: لأن أقرأ البقرة أرتلها أحب إلي من أن أقرأ القرآن كله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid explains tartīl as reading slowly and deliberately.
rows.anchor: ترسل فيه ترسلا عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda explains tartīl as reading with steadiness and deliberation.
rows.anchor: تثبت فيه تثبتا عن قتادة

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: ʿAlī says not to rush like poetry or scatter like sand, but to strike hard hearts and not merely aim to finish a surah.
rows.anchor: بينه بيانا ولا تهذه هذ الشعر ولا تنثره نثر الرمل

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh says to ask God for Paradise at verses mentioning it and seek refuge from Hell at verses mentioning it.
rows.anchor: إذا مررت بآية فيها ذكر الجنة فاسأل الله الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says tartīl means reading in sequence without changing wording or moving later material ahead.
rows.anchor: الترتيل هو أن تقرأ على نظمه وتواليه ولا تغير لفظا ولا تقدم مؤخرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This explanation derives tartīl from evenly arranged teeth and a gap-free, well-ordered set of teeth.
rows.anchor: مأخوذ من ترتل الأسنان إذا استوت وحسن انتظامها

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Quṭrub says ratl means softness, so tartīl here calls for a sorrowful tone.
rows.anchor: رتل معناه ضعف والرتل اللين عن قطرب

rows.speaker: أبو بصير
rows.claim: Abū Baṣīr reports from Abū ʿAbd Allāh that tartīl means lingering over verses and beautifying the voice.
rows.anchor: ما رواه أبو بصير عن أبي عبد الله ع في هذا

rows.speaker: أم سلمة
rows.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet paused his recitation verse by verse.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أم سلمة أنها قالت: كان رسول الله

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet prolonged his voice in recitation.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس قال كان يمد صوته مدا

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports the Prophet's promise that the Qurʾan's companion will be told to recite and rise, with rank at the last verse read.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن عمر قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل والحسن
rows.claim: They say revelation burdens the Prophet through conveying it, harm, night prayer, self-discipline, and foregoing rest; it burdens the community through commands, prohibitions, and legal limits.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول قتادة ومقاتل والحسن

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd calls the revelation weighty and blessed, with its weight showing in the scales on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: هو والله ثقيل مبارك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says only a divinely supported heart and a soul supported by monotheism can bear the revelation.
rows.anchor: ثقيلا لا يحمله إلا قلب مؤيد بالتوفيق ونفس مؤيدة بالتوحيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says it is weighty because it is not trivial or frivolous: it is God's speech.
rows.anchor: ثقيلا ليس بالسفساف الخفيف لأنه كلام ربنا جلت عظمته عن الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation calls it weighty in stature, like sound speech that has weight when fittingly placed.
rows.anchor: معناه قولا عظيم الشأن كما يقال هذا كلام رصين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation was physically arduous: the Prophet's state changed, he sweated, and his mounted camel would kneel and become unable to walk.
rows.anchor: قولا ثقيلا نزوله فإنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يتغير حاله عند نزوله ويعرق

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Asked by al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām how revelation came, the Prophet described a bell-like sound as hardest, or an angel appearing as a man.
rows.anchor: وسأل الحرث بن هشام رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا رسول الله كيف يأتيك الوحي

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says revelation came to the Prophet even while mounted; on a very cold day it ended with sweat pouring from his brow.
rows.anchor: قالت عائشة إنه كان ليوحى إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو على راحلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says revelation is weighty for unbelievers because it exposes their ignorance, error, foolishness, and ugly deeds.
rows.anchor: ثقيلا على الكفار لما فيه من الكشف عن جهلهم وضلالهم وسفه أحلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāshiʾat al-layl means night hours, which arise one after another.
rows.anchor: ساعات الليل لأنها تنشأ ساعة بعد ساعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says it means the whole night because it follows the day.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هو الليل كله لأنه ينشأ بعد النهار

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says it means the night hours devoted to tahajjud.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد هي ساعات التهجد من الليل

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr say the word is Abyssinian for standing at night.
rows.anchor: هي بالحبشية قيام الليل عن عبد الله بن مسعود وسعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾisha says nāshiʾa is rising after sleep.
rows.anchor: القيام بعد النوم عن عائشة

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda say it means prayer after the late evening prayer.
rows.anchor: ما كان بعد العشاء الآخرة عن الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh say it is rising at the end of night for night prayer.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جعفر وأبي عبد الله ع أنهما قالا: هي القيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With waṭʾ, the phrase means night prayer is weightier and more difficult because work is harder during the usual time for rest.
rows.anchor: أي أكثر ثقلا وأبلغ مشقة لأن الليل وقت الراحة والعمل يشق فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With waṭāʾ, it means the heart, tongue, hearing, and sight align in understanding and reflection because worldly distractions are absent.
rows.anchor: ومن قال وطاء فالمعنى أشد مواطأة للسمع والبصر يتوافق فيها قلب المصلي

rows.speaker: أنس ومجاهد وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain aqwamu qīlan as more correct recitation and firmer speech because the mind is free from distraction.
rows.anchor: القلب عن أنس ومجاهد وابن زيد

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh says this is a person's rising from bed seeking nothing but God.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله ع هو قيام الرجل عن فراشه لا يريد به إلا الله

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the Prophet has the day for going about and attending to his needs.
rows.anchor: معناه أن لك يا محمد في النهار منصرفا ومنقلبا إلى ما تقضي فيه حوائجك عن قتادة

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's daytime duties include conveying the message, calling people, teaching obligations and practices, and providing for his family; night frees the heart for remembrance and recitation.
rows.anchor: فإنك تحتاج فيه إلى تبليغ الرسالة ودعوة الخلق وتعليم الفرائض والسنن وإصلاح المعيشة

words: إِنَّ لَكَ فِى ٱلنَّهَارِ سَبْحًۭا طَوِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Teaching and learning do not excuse neglecting night prayer: the Prophet had greater teaching demands yet did not forgo his share.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دلالة على أنه لا عذر لأحد في ترك صلاة الليل لأجل التعليم والتعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remember God by invoking His names, through which worship is performed in supplication.
rows.anchor: يعني أسماء الله تعالى التي تعبد بالدعاء بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is to recite the basmala at prayer's start so its blessing connects the reciter to God and separates him from all else.
rows.anchor: اقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم في ابتداء صلاتك توصلك بركة قراءتها إلى ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to direct one's deeds toward God's pleasure.
rows.anchor: واقصد بعملك وجه ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others explain tabattul as sincere devotion in supplication and worship.
rows.anchor: أخلص له إخلاصا عن ابن عباس وغيره يعني في الدعاء والعبادة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says tabattul means turning wholly to God, the root sense.
rows.anchor: انقطع إليه انقطاعا عن عطاء وهو الأصل

rows.speaker: شقيق
rows.claim: Shafīq explains tabattul as relying on God.
rows.anchor: توكل عليه توكلا عن شقيق

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains tabattul as devoting oneself to worship.
rows.anchor: تفرغ لعبادته عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition on tabattul refers to withdrawing from people and communal gatherings; here the Prophet is to devote himself to God.
rows.anchor: والمراد به الانقطاع عن الناس والجماعات وكان يجب أن يقول تبتلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says tabtīlan is used to match the endings of the surah's verses.
rows.anchor: إنما قال تبتيلا ليطابق أواخر آيات السورة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh say tabattul here means raising the hands in prayer.
rows.anchor: أن التبتل هنا رفع اليدين في الصلاة

rows.speaker: أبو بصير
rows.claim: Abū Baṣīr says tabattul is raising one's hands to God and beseeching Him.
rows.anchor: هو رفع يدك إلى الله وتضرعك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view calls God Lord of the whole world, since it lies between east and west.
rows.anchor: أي رب العالم بما فيه لأنه بين المشرق والمغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view refers to the sun's rising and setting, assigning the first half of the day to the east and the second to the west.
rows.anchor: رب مشرق الشمس ومغربها والمراد أول النهار وآخره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view glosses the phrase as owner and controller of the regions between east and west.
rows.anchor: مالك المشرق والمغرب أي المتصرف فيما بينهما والمدبر لما بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God is entitled to be worshipped.
rows.anchor: لا أحد تحق له العبادة سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Take God as guardian who manages and attends to your affairs.
rows.anchor: أي حفيظا للقيام بأمرك

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأهل الكوفة
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and the Kufans read half and a third in the accusative.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأهل الكوفة نصفه وثلثه بالنصب

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The remaining readers use the genitive for half and a third.
rows.anchor: والباقون بالجر

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the accusative reading attaches half and a third to adnā, itself accusative.
rows.anchor: من نصب حمله على أدنى وأدنى في موضع نصب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda says adnā means nearer, yielding the sense that one also stands half and a third of the night.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة أدنى أقرب فكأنه قال

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan objects that this cannot mean nearer than half and a third; he understands it as less than those amounts.
rows.anchor: وليس المعنى عليه فيما بلغنا لأن المعنى يكون على أدنى من نصفه

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: For the genitive reading, Abū al-Ḥasan understands a concession to pray less than the required amount.
rows.anchor: فأما الذين قرؤوا بالجر فعلى أن يكون المعنى إنكم إن لم تؤدوا ما فرض الله عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adnā means nearer to, or less than, two thirds; the pronoun refers to night, with prayer near two thirds on some nights and near half or a third on others.
rows.anchor: الهاء تعود إلى الليل أي نصف الليل وثلث الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes the pronoun refer to two thirds, making the prayer nearer to half or a third of that amount.
rows.anchor: إن الهاء تعود إلى الثلثين أي وأقرب من نصف الثلثين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the accusative reading, the phrase means standing half and a third of the night.
rows.anchor: وإذا نصبت فالمعنى تقوم نصفه وثلثه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the accompanying group as Abū ʿAlī and Abū Dharr.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله { وطائفة من الذين معك } قال أبو علي وأبو ذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God apportions night and day so people can act during them as commanded.
rows.anchor: يقدر أوقاتهما لتعملوا فيها على ما يأمركم به

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ says the meaning is that God misses none of what people do.
rows.anchor: لا يفوته علم ما تفعلون عن عطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse means God knows how much of the night people will stand in prayer.
rows.anchor: يعلم القدر الذي تقومونه من الليل

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says people prayed at night fearing they would fail to reach the commanded amount, so God says they cannot calculate it precisely.
rows.anchor: كان الرجل يصلي الليل مخافة أن لا يصيب ما أمر به من القيام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says they prayed until their feet swelled, and God told them they could not truly keep count.
rows.anchor: قاموا حتى انتفخت أقدامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that they could not sustain night prayer consistently and would fall short.
rows.anchor: لن تطيقوا المداومة على قيام الليل ويقع منكم التقصير فيه

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says God made night prayer voluntary rather than obligatory.
rows.anchor: بأن جعله تطوعا ولم يجعله فرضا عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means no liability is imposed, or that God eased the burden.
rows.anchor: فتاب عليكم أي فخفف عليكم

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes take the command as reciting whatever is manageable in night prayer.
rows.anchor: يعني في صلاة الليل عن أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says the earlier command to stand means rising to recite the Qurʾan, not necessarily to pray.
rows.anchor: أراد القيام لقراءة القرآن لا غير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say to pray whatever is manageable, calling prayer Qurʾan because it includes recitation.
rows.anchor: فصلوا ما تيسر من الصلاة وعبر عن الصلاة بالقرآن لأنها تتضمنه

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes treat recitation outside prayer as recommended, not obligatory, since obligation would entail memorization.
rows.anchor: محمول على الاستحباب عند الأكثرين دون الوجوب لأنه لو وجبت القراءة لوجب الحفظ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some hold recitation obligatory because it reveals the Qurʾan's inimitability and proofs of monotheism and prophethood, while memorization remains recommended.
rows.anchor: محمول على الوجوب لأن القارىء يقف على إعجاز القرآن وما فيه من دلائل التوحيد

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the manageable amount is fifty verses.
rows.anchor: فقال سعيد بن جبير خمسون آية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the manageable amount is one hundred verses.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس مائة آية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says whoever reads one hundred verses in a night will not have the Qurʾan litigate against him.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن قال: من قرأ مائة آية في ليلة

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: Kaʿb says reading one hundred verses in a night counts a person among the devout.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب: من قرأ مائة آية في ليلة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says the amount is two hundred verses.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: مائتا آية

rows.speaker: جويبر
rows.claim: Juwaybir says it is a third of the Qurʾan, since God made recitation easy for His servants.
rows.anchor: وقال جويبر: ثلث القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning is an amount of recitation that a person wants and finds agreeable.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن معنى ما تيسر مقدار ما أردتم وأحببتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prospect of illness is one reason God gives for easing night prayer.
rows.anchor: ذلك يقتضي التخفيف عنكم

words: يَضْرِبُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ يَبْتَغُونَ مِن فَضْلِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains traveling in God's bounty as journeys for trade and profit.
rows.anchor: يسافرون للتجارة وطلب الأرباح عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers fighting in God's path are another reason for easing the night prayer.
rows.anchor: فكل ذلك يقتضي التخفيف عنكم

rows.speaker: الرضا
rows.claim: Al-Riḍā, quoting his father and grandfather, says manageable recitation is what brings humility of heart and purity of inner self.
rows.anchor: عن الرضا ع عن أبيه عن جده ع قال ما تيسر منه لكم فيه خشوع القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establish prayer according to the limits God made obligatory.
rows.anchor: بحدودها التي أوجبها الله عليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zakat commanded here is obligatory alms.
rows.anchor: المفروضة { وأقرضوا الله قرضا حسنا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lending God a good loan means spending in God's cause and in causes He commands or encourages.
rows.anchor: أنفقوا في سبيل الله والجهات التي أمركم الله وندبكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What people send ahead is obedience; they will find its reward with God, better than miserliness and shortcoming.
rows.anchor: أي طاعة { تجدوه } أي تجدوا ثوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Huwa may be an emphatic separator, called faṣl by Basrans and ʿimād by Kufans, or an adjective of the object pronoun.
rows.anchor: يسمى فصلا عند البصريين وعمادا عند الكوفيين ويجوز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking forgiveness means asking God to forgive; He covers sins, pardons, and shows mercy.
rows.anchor: { واستغفروا الله } أي اطلبوا مغفرته

words: يَضْرِبُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ يَبْتَغُونَ مِن فَضْلِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says a patient, God-seeking merchant who brings goods to a Muslim city and sells at the day's price is like the martyrs.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن مسعود: أيما رجل جلب شيئا

words: يَضْرِبُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ يَبْتَغُونَ مِن فَضْلِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says that after dying in God's path, he would most wish to die traveling while seeking God's bounty.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عمر: ما خلق الله موتة أموتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the verse is Medinan because prayer and zakat were not made obligatory in Mecca.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مدنية ويدل عليها أن الصلاة والزكاة لم توجبا بمكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says prayer and zakat were already obligatory in Mecca, so the verse is Meccan.
rows.anchor: أوجبتا بمكة والآية مكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the Prophet had wrapped himself in a small cloak to sleep and was addressed as a sleeper told to rise and warn his people.
rows.anchor: كان قد تدثر بشملة صغيرة لينام فقال يا أيها النائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation calls for energetic effort, fulfilling the mission without idleness; Arabs say a person does not sleep over a serious task.
rows.anchor: إن المراد به الجد في الأمر والقيام بما أرسل به وترك الهوينا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples describe resolve and sleepless effort until a need or vengeance is achieved.
rows.anchor: أرى كل ذي وتر يقوم بوتره ويمنع عنه النوم إذ أنت نائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ish timāl means the same as tadaththur, wrapping oneself in a garment.
rows.anchor: والاشتمال مثل التدثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Magnify your Lord by exalting Him and declaring Him above anything unbefitting.
rows.anchor: أي عظمه ونزهه عما لا يليق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to say Allāhu akbar in prayer.
rows.anchor: كبره في الصلاة فقل الله أكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation commands washing the clothes worn in prayer to remove impurity.
rows.anchor: وثيابك الملبوسة فطهرها من النجاسة للصلاة

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Qatāda and Mujāhid take garments as a metaphor for the self, to be purified from sins; grammatically, the possessor is omitted.
rows.anchor: ونفسك فطهر من الذنوب والثياب عبارة عن النفس عن قتادة ومجاهد

rows.speaker: عنترة
rows.claim: ʿAntara's line uses garments figuratively for the person pierced by a spear, supporting the garment-as-self interpretation.
rows.anchor: قول عنترة: فشككت بالرمح الأصم ثيابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says to keep clothing free of sin or treachery; al-Zajjāj notes the Arab expression that a traitor has dirty garments.
rows.anchor: طهر ثيابك من لبسها على معصية أو غدرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās cites Salāma ibn Ghaylān's line that he never wore a wicked garment or concealed treachery.
rows.anchor: أنشده ابن عباس: وإني بحمد الله لا ثوب فاجر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says a righteous man is called pure in garments and a wicked one foul in garments, so the verse calls for correcting deeds.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: يقال للرجل إذا كان صالحا إنه لطاهر الثياب

rows.speaker: طاووس
rows.claim: Ṭāwūs explains the command as shortening clothes so they do not drag into dirt.
rows.anchor: وثيابك فقصر عن طاووس

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: A report from Abū ʿAbd Allāh also explains it as shortening clothes, which avoids dirt from dragging hems.
rows.anchor: عن إبي عبد الله ع قال الزجاج: لأن تقصير الثوب

rows.speaker: ابن زيد وابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and Ibn Sīrīn say to wash clothing of impurity because polytheists did not purify themselves.
rows.anchor: وثيابك فاغسلها عن النجاسة بالماء لأن المشركين كانوا لا يتطهرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says clothing should not be acquired unlawfully.
rows.anchor: لا تكن ثيابك من حرام عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says to purify one's wives from disbelief and sin; Arabs use garments as a euphemism for women.
rows.anchor: حتى يصرن مؤمنات صالحات والعرب تكني بالثياب عن النساء عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: أمير المؤمنين
rows.claim: ʿAlī says washing garments removes worry and sadness and purifies the prayer place; rolling up clothes purifies it too.
rows.anchor: غسل الثياب يذهب الهم والحزن وهو طهور المصلاة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والزهري
rows.claim: They say to shun idols and images.
rows.anchor: اهجر الأصنام والأوثان عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والزهري

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says to avoid sins.
rows.anchor: اجتنب المعاصي عن الحسن

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī distinguishes kasra as punishment and ḍamma as idol, so the command means avoiding what leads to punishment; other linguists make no distinction.
rows.anchor: الرجز بالكسر العذاب وبالضم الصنم وقال المعنى اهجر ما يؤدي إلى العذاب

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī says to avoid ugly actions and bad character.
rows.anchor: جانب الفعل القبيح والخلق الذميم عن الجبائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says to remove love of worldly life from the heart because it is the source of every sin.
rows.anchor: أخرج حب الدنيا من قلبك لأنه رأس كل خطيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks why they turn away from the Qurʾan's admonitions; if they reject it, they have nothing awaiting them in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: أي أي شيء لهم ولم أعرضوا وتولوا عن القرآن فلم يؤمنوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image is of wild asses fleeing in alarm.
rows.anchor: كأنهم حمر وحشية نافرة

rows.speaker: عطاء والكلبي
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and al-Kalbī identify the qaswara as a lion.
rows.anchor: يعني الأسد عن عطاء والكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās compares unbelievers fleeing the Qurʾan when the Prophet recites to wild asses fleeing after seeing a lion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: الحمر الوحشية إذا عاينت الأسد هربت منه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك ومقاتل ومجاهد
rows.claim: An alternative view from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqātil, and Mujāhid takes qaswara as archers or hunting men.
rows.anchor: القسورة الرماة ورجال القنص عن ابن عباس بخلاف والضحاك ومقاتل ومجاهد

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr identifies qaswara as hunters.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير هم القناص

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say each person wants a heavenly book addressed to him by name, commanding belief in Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: تنزل إليهم بأسمائهم أن آمنوا بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم عن الحسن وقتادة وابن زيد

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they demand written guarantees against punishment and promises of blessing even while persisting in disbelief.
rows.anchor: يريدون صحفا من الله تعالى بالبراءة من العقوبة وإسباغ النعمة

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says each wants to be a prophet receiving revelation and having followers, refusing to be a follower.
rows.anchor: يريد كل واحد منهم أن يكون رسولا يوحى إليه متبوعا وأنف من أن يكون تابعا

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand for written pages explains their earlier demand for a book from heaven to read.
rows.anchor: ولن نؤمن لرقيك حتى تنزل علينا كتابا نقرؤه

words: بَلْ يُرِيدُ كُلُّ ٱمْرِئٍۢ مِنْهُمْ أَن يُؤْتَىٰ صُحُفًۭا مُّنَشَّرَةًۭ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rejects their demand: events will not happen as they propose.
rows.anchor: أي حقا ليس الأمر على ما قالوا ولا يكون كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They reject the reality of the afterlife; if they feared its punishment, they would not demand signs after proofs and miracles were established.
rows.anchor: بجحدهم صحتها ولو خافوا عذاب الآخرة لما اقترحوا الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā affirms that the Qurʾan is a reminder and admonition.
rows.anchor: أي إن القرآن تذكير وموعظة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whoever wishes may take heed from the Qurʾan, since doing so is within that person's capacity.
rows.anchor: اتعظ به لأنه قادر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second mention of will differs from the first to avoid contradiction: the first is voluntary choice, the second compulsion, so unbelievers heed only if God compels them.
rows.anchor: هذه المشيئة غير الأولى إذ لو كانت واحدة لتناقض فالأولى مشيئة اختيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation makes God's will His commands, prohibitions, promises, and warnings; human willing follows God's prior will.
rows.anchor: إلا أن يشاء الله من حيث أمر به ونهى عن تركه ووعد الثواب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says God is worthy to have His prohibitions observed and worthy to forgive sins.
rows.anchor: هو أهل أن يتقى محارمه وأهل أن يغفر الذنوب عن قتادة

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report traced to the Prophet through Anas says the Prophet recited this verse; no further report content is supplied here.
rows.anchor: وروي مرفوعا عن أنس قال: إن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم تلا هذه الآية
